chunks: From him, from Hammad, from Shu'ayb, from Abu Basir, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about purchasing lands from the Ahl al-Dhimma (People of the Covenant), so he said: 'There is no harm in purchasing from them if they work it and revive it, for it belongs to them. And the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was victorious over Khaybar, and the Jews were in it; he expelled them according to a matter (command) and left the land in their hands, so they worked it and cultivated it.'

key_terms.أَهْلِ ٱلذِّمَّةِ: People of the Covenant (non-Muslims living under Muslim rule)
key_terms.خَيْبَرَ: Khaybar (a historical region known for its fertile land and Jewish inhabitants)
key_terms.عَمِلُوهَا وَأَحْيَوْهَا: They work it and revive it (cultivate and develop)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to buy land from non-Muslims in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes the permissibility of purchasing agricultural lands from Ahl al-Dhimma, contingent upon their active cultivation and revival of the soil, thereby affirming their ownership rights. He grounds this ruling in the Prophetic precedent of the Conquest of Khaybar, where the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) retained the Jewish tribes on their lands to work them, illustrating a model of coexistence and economic integration within the Islamic state. This hadith is pivotal in Shia jurisprudence for distinguishing between land ownership and sovereignty, emphasizing that productive use validates private property rights even for non-Muslims under Muslim rule.
